title: Two Isosceles Triangles, One Mystery Angle | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: The figure (bank SVG scaled up). Line 1: the 24° mark glows, then a '?' appears at the top angle A. Line 2: two tick marks on AB and AC, and two (different style) on BD and BC. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: We know just one angle, twenty-four degrees. Can we find the angle at the top?
The secret is hiding in two isosceles triangles.
Hi, I'm Vantee, your math tutor! Let's go on an angle chase.

scenes.visual: Question text left, figure right. Line 2: AB and AC flash with single tick marks. Line 3: D pulses on side AC; BD and BC flash with double tick marks. Line 4: angle ABD marked '24°'. Line 5: angle BAC marked '?'. Line 6: choice chips 22°, 24°, 34°, 36°, 44°.
lines: Here's the question.
In triangle A B C, side A B equals side A C.
Point D is on side A C, so that B D equals B C.
Angle A B D is twenty-four degrees.
What is the measure of angle B A C, the angle at the top?
Here are the five choices.

scenes.visual: Line 1: triangle ABC shaded light green with tag 'isosceles: AB = AC'. Line 2: triangle BDC shaded light purple with tag 'isosceles: BD = BC'. Line 3: tag 'goal: angle A'.
lines: So we have two isosceles triangles. The big one, A B C, has two equal sides from A.
The small one, B D C, has two equal sides from B.
Our goal is the top angle, at A.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; figure and question visible.
lines: Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Figure left, equation rows right. Line 1: angle A labeled 'a'. Line 2: equal sides AB, AC tick-marked; the two base angles at B (whole angle ABC) and C both get the same arc color. Line 3: row 'a + C + C = 180' → 'C = 90 − a/2' (use \dfrac{a}{2}), and angle C labeled with it.
lines: Welcome back! Let's name what we don't know. Call the top angle a.
Side A B equals side A C, so the angles at B and C are equal. Those are the base angles.
The three angles add to one hundred eighty, so each base angle is ninety minus half of a.

scenes.visual: Line 1: triangle BDC highlighted; BD and BC tick-marked; angle BDC gets the same arc color as angle C, labeled 'C'. Line 2: row 'angle DBC = 180 − C − C'. Line 3: row '= 180 − (180 − a) = a', and angle DBC labeled 'a' in the same color as the top angle. Line 4: both 'a' angles pulse together (aha beat).
lines: Now the small triangle. B D equals B C, so the angles at D and C match. Angle B D C equals angle C.
So angle D B C is one hundred eighty, minus angle C, minus angle C.
Two base angles add to one hundred eighty minus a. So angle D B C is just a!
Look at that. The little angle at B is the same as the top angle.

scenes.visual: Line 1: angle ABC split into '24°' and 'a', row 'angle ABC = 24 + a'. Line 2: row '24 + a = 90 − a/2'. Line 3: row 'a + a/2 = 66' (66 = 90 − 24 shown). Line 4: 'one and a half a = 66 → a = 44' answer badge '44°', chime at end of line, choice E highlighted. Line 5: check row 'C = 68, 68 − 44 = 24 ✓'.
lines: Angle A B C is made of two parts: twenty-four degrees, plus a.
But angle A B C is also a base angle. So twenty-four plus a equals ninety minus half of a.
Add half of a to both sides, and take away twenty-four. One and a half a equals sixty-six.
So a is forty-four degrees. That's Choice E!
Check: each base angle is sixty-eight. And sixty-eight minus forty-four is twenty-four. It works!

scenes.visual: Fresh figure. Line 1: triangle ABD highlighted; angle BDC (outside it, at D) marked. Line 2: rule card 'outside angle = sum of the two far inside angles'. Line 3: row 'angle BDC = a + 24'. Line 4: angle C labeled 'a + 24' too (BD = BC); angle ABC also 'a + 24'. Line 5: rows '(a + 24) + (a + 24) + a = 180', '3a + 48 = 180', '3a = 132', 'a = 44'. Line 6: small text 'no fractions!'.
lines: Here's another way, with no fractions. Look at triangle A B D, on the left.
An outside angle of a triangle equals the two inside angles far from it.
So angle B D C equals a plus twenty-four.
Angle C matches angle B D C, so it's a plus twenty-four too. And so is angle A B C.
The big triangle adds up: three a plus forty-eight is one hundred eighty.
So three a is one hundred thirty-two, and a is forty-four.
When would you pick this way? When you spot an outside angle. It saves a step.

scenes.visual: A test table: columns 'top angle a', 'base angle C', 'angle DBC = a', 'angle ABD = C − a'. Rows fill as discussed: 24 → 78 → 54 (red); 36 → 72 → 36 (red); 22 → 79 → 57 (red); 34 → 73 → 39 (red); 44 → 68 → 24 (green). Line 1: chip B '24° = angle ABD'.
lines: Now the traps. Choice B, twenty-four, is the angle we were given.
It's not the one we were asked for.
Here's a quick test for any choice.
Find the base angle, then subtract the top angle. You should get twenty-four.
Try twenty-four on top.
The base angle is seventy-eight, and seventy-eight minus twenty-four is fifty-four. Too big.
Choice D, thirty-six, comes from a famous triangle
with angles thirty-six, seventy-two and seventy-two. But here it gives thirty-six, not twenty-four.
Choices A and C, twenty-two and thirty-four, give fifty-seven and thirty-nine. Neither works.
Only forty-four gives exactly twenty-four.

scenes.visual: Same figure setup (redrawn with apex 40°, so proportions differ slightly), angle ABD labeled '30°', top angle '?'. Tick marks AB = AC and BD = BC.
lines: Ready for a challenge? Same setup: A B equals A C, and B D equals B C.
This time, angle A B D is thirty degrees. What is the top angle?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant figure visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows per line on the variant figure: 'outside angle BDC = a + 30'; 'C = a + 30, angle ABC = a + 30'; '3a + 60 = 180 → 3a = 120 → a = 40' answer badge '40°' chime at end of that line; check 'C = 70, 70 − 40 = 30 ✓'.
lines: Let's check. The outside angle at D is a plus thirty.
So angle C and angle A B C are both a plus thirty.
The angles add up: three a plus sixty is one hundred eighty. So three a is one hundred twenty.
The top angle is forty degrees!
Check: the base angles are seventy. Seventy minus forty is thirty. Yes!
If you got forty degrees, superb angle chasing!

scenes.visual: Summary card: the figure with both isosceles triangles shaded, 'equal sides → equal angles', 'name the unknown, chase it around'.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
Equal sides mean equal angles.
Name the unknown angle with a letter, and chase it from triangle to triangle.
This is Vantee, signing off. Keep chasing, and I'll see you next time!
